paragraphs.text: 1.2(1) The purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and a cost-effective way. … In particular, these rules are intended to be used to identify the real issues in dispute … to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense … and so on. 9 I find that the Master has erred in law for the reasons set out in the appellant's brief. It is clear to me, as argued by the appellant, that the Master's order artificially limits questioning by Cenovus, creates unnecessary delay, undermines the efficiency and cost-effectiveness, and prejudices Cenovus' ability to obtain information. In short, the Master erred in not allowing the questioning to occur concurrently, based on the availability of witnesses, which is the norm in litigation, and to my knowledge has never been other than what has been indicated in the appellant's brief. It is for all of these reasons that the appeal is granted, and there are costs in favour of the appellant on the normal schedule. 8. Questions Going to Credibility In Yeung v. Yeung (1993), 137 A.R. 303 (Master), the plaintiff commenced an action in replevin, alleging that the defendant had stolen certain items from the plaintiff. In examinations for discovery, the defendant was examined as to her criminal record and the plaintiff sought an order of the court compelling the defendant to produce medical records which allegedly would show that the defendant suffered from a mental disorder. In dismissing the application, Master Funduk, at p. 306 said: Clearly this is an abuse of an examination for discovery. This is information sought to show that the defendant is not credible. But matters going solely to credibility cannot be the subject of examinations for discovery. What is the connection between those convictions and this replevin action. There is none. The medical testimony in the criminal proceedings is also not relevant. It is sought to show that the defendant is a thief. It is sought to show that she is not credible. It is an attack on the defendant's credibility by an attack on her character. That cannot be done on an examination for discovery where the person being examined does not raise her character as an issue in her pleading. 9. Questions about the Identity of a Witness In Hailmichael v. Roodzant (1998), 72 Alta. L.R. (3d) 350 (Master), the plaintiff in a motor vehicle accident action, the trial of which was scheduled to last two weeks, learned that the defendant had located someone who claimed to have seen the accident occur. The defendant would not disclose the name of the witness. The plaintiff brought an application to compel disclosure. In granting the order sought, Master Waller acknowledged that “the general rule is that the names of witnesses need not be disclosed” (p. 351). However, the learned Master noted an exception: the name will have to be disclosed “if the name of the person is a relevant fact in the case”. That exception is itself qualified because disclosure will not be ordered “where the disclosure of the name of a witness might adversely effect (sic) that party” (p. 351). Master Waller then reviewed the law in Alberta, and noted that “there can be no doubt that the prevalent judicial view requires full disclosure through the discovery process” (p. 354). In refusing to follow previous decisions, and ordering disclosure of the witness's name, the learned Master said, at pp. 354-55: This requirement of full disclosure has manifested a number of rule changes including rules dealing with the disclosure of evidence of experts. Indeed the Rules of Court Committee of the Law Society of Alberta have recommended changes to Practice Note No. 3 to allow a pre-trial conference [justice] to direct the disclosure of names of all witnesses proposed to be called. The law is never static, it changes with the times and evolves to deal with current realities. The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in Soke Farm Equipment Ltd. v. New Holland of Canada Ltd., [1990] 2 W.W.R. 762 (Sask. C.A.) after carefully reviewing this history of the rule against the disclosure of the names of witnesses conclude that the rule has no place in modern jurisprudence… I prefer the reasoning of the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal … The Court must be practical. The prospect of a two week trial might well be obviated by the disclosure of the name of the independ[e]nt witness. A settlement is more likely to be affected [sic] with blinkers off rather than blinkers on. Counsel for the Respondent says that the rules of stare decisis require me to follow the 1946 decision in [Sembrat v. Milligan, [1946] 1 W.W.R. 517 (Alta. T.D.)]. The doctrine is never absolute and Sembrat is out of step with modern litigation practice. 10. Duty of Employees to Inform Themselves The broad principle in the Opron Construction case [Opron Construction Ltd. v. Alberta (1990), 71 Alta. L.R. (2d) 28 (C.A.)] is that an employee may be asked his opinion if the pleadings put into issue the opinion of the witnesses in question. Although not specifically stated, it seems to me it is not unreasonable to expect that in those circumstances an employee must also inform himself. The reason given by Côté, J.A., in Opron Construction for the opinion rule seems to me to apply just as aptly to the duty to inform rule namely “Otherwise a corporation sued for its employee's incompetence might bar key discovery by naming him as its officer for discovery”…Insul Fibre Ltd. v. Strathcona Mechanical Alberta Ltd. (1991), 116 A.R. 304 (Master), at 305, per Master Breitkreuz. 11. Duty to Inform (General Statement) In Wright v. Schultz (1992), 135 A.R. 58 (C.A.), Hetherington J.A., at p. 63: Must the appellant seek information from others? In my view an individual who is examined for discovery must inform himself of matters within the knowledge of anyone over whom he has control and he must inform himself of matters within the knowledge of his employees and agents. In relation to employees the case of McLean v. Canadian Pacific Railway (1916), 10 W.W.R. 949 (Alta. C.A.), contains obiter dicta to this effect. In that case Mr. Justice Beck, writing for the majority, said at p. 951: In the case of the examination for discovery of an individual litigant he, equally with an officer of a corporation, is under the English practice bound to inform himself of the matters within the knowledge of his employees, … I should think he is equally bound to do so under our rules; … See also Medicine Hat Wheat Co. v. Norris Commission Co. (1916), 10 W.W.R. 1,092 at p. 1,093 (Alta. C.A.). In my opinion an individual who is examined for discovery must also inform himself of matters within the knowledge of his agent. In Canadian Utilities Ltd. v. Mannix Ltd. et al. (1959), 29 W.W.R.(N.S.) 289 (Alta. C.A.), the court required the officer of a corporation to seek information from an engineer as to knowledge acquired by the engineer while he was acting as the agent of the corporation. Similarly I think that an individual should be required to seek information from his agent. The law in this regard is correctly stated by Mr. Justice McDonald in [Tiedemann v. Basiuk (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 12 (Q.B.)] at pp. 14, 15. He said: The party being examined is not bound to inquire of third persons over whom he has no control: … Conversely, he is bound to inform himself as to matters in question within the knowledge of his servants or agents: … And if the person being examined is an officer of a corporation, he must get such information as he can from other officers and servants of the corporation who have personal knowledge of the facts: … This statement of the law was applied in Turkawski v. 738675 Alberta Ltd., 2005 ABQB 423, 2005 CarswellAlta 793, 372 A.R. 7 at pp 13-14. 12. What To Do When an Undertaking Is Not Met In K. (P.E.) v. K. (B.W.), 2004 ABCA 135, 2003 CarswellAlta 1936, 348 A.R. 77, Wittmann J.A. said, at p. 79: The proper procedure for a claimant to follow when there has been no response to an undertaking is to make an application seeking the court to compel the delinquent party to respond to the order. If the party then fails to respond, he or she may be held in civil contempt: Carr (L.P.) Professional Corp. v. Ascot Engineering Ltd. (1988), 93 A.R. 269 (Q.B. Master). 13. Must One Answer Undertakings Prior to the Conclusion of the Discovery? In Ho v. Computeraid Professional Services Ltd., 2007 ABQB 36, 2007 CarswellAlta 41, 72 Alta. L.R. (4th) 183 (Master), an examination for discovery had been adjourned because insufficient time had been allotted for its completion. Prior to the resumption of the examination for discovery, the applicant requested responses to the undertakings which had been given so far in the discovery. The respondent refused, and an application for an order compelling answers to the undertakings was sought. Master Waller dismissed the application, and said: 4 I agree that the general rule ought to be that undertakings need not be responded to until the discovery is concluded subject only to further examination arising from the undertakings. This only makes practical sense. It prevents litigation by bifurcated installments and lessens the demands on valuable court time. 5 As with any general rule there may be exceptions. If a proper area of discovery is foreclosed by a refusal to undertake to obtain relevant information the examining party would be permitted to bring an application without concluding the discovery. 6 Further counsel might agree to the provision of undertakings prior to concluding the discovery. Such agreement are invariably recognized by the courts. 7 Finally a discovery where the examined party is a totally uniformed officer might well not be concluded until that officer has gone back and become properly informed. 8 This list of exceptions should be regarded as illustrative rather than exhaustive as no court can attempt to deal with every fact contingency that might arise. In Jetco Heavy Duty Lighting v. Fonteyne, 2012 ABQB 211, 2012 CarswellAlta 546, Master Breitkreuz quoted with approval from Master Waller's decision in Ho v. Computeraid Professional Services Ltd., and at paragraph 10, the learned Master said: … To provide undertakings and attend for cross-examination on those undertakings after discoveries are completed is a well-established and time-honoured practice in this province. If the authors of the new Rules of Court intended a departure from that practice, I suggest it would have been specifically addressed somewhere in Part 5. 14. “Opinion Questions” Questions which elicit a witness' opinion where, as here, his professional or technical competence and conduct are clearly at issue are permitted …Drake v. Overland (1979), 19 A.R. 472 at 484 (C.A.). Opinion questions must relate to an issue of the competence of the witness. An infant plaintiff sues her doctor alleging that he was negligent in treating her. The father is the next friend and he just happens to also be a doctor. The County would say that the father could be required to answer questions about his medical knowledge and his opinions based on his medical knowledge. That of course is wrong. The father's “professional or technical competence and conduct” are not directly or indirectly at issue. In that example it is just a coincidence that the father is a doctor, just as it is a coincidence that in this lawsuit that the father is a professional engineer and has an expertise in road projects. That coincidence cannot be a footing to give the county something that it does not otherwise have. I also do not think that Catre Industries v. Alberta (1984), 54 A.R. 277 (Q.B.), relied on by counsel for the County, assists it. The County relies on the following quote, p. 279, where the chambers judge after referring to Czuy says: It is clear from this decision that the Alberta Court of Appeal has not limited the ‘opinion rule’ on examinations for discovery to cases involving professional malpractice or to cases where the cause of action involves the standard of care required of a professional individual. In fact, the Alberta Court of Appeal directed that questions relating both to the competence of the plaintiff as a hockey coach, which was the subject matter of the defamation, and the competence of the defendant as a hockey reporter be answered, even though both required expressions of opinion on the part of the witness. In the Drake matter no question arose as to whether corporate officers are bound to answer the same question when produced on behalf of the corporate defendant. The Alberta Court of Appeal, however, made it clear that in cases where professional and technical competence or conduct were in issue, opinion evidence could be elicited. Again, I do not have a quarrel with that, but it does not assist the County. Again, the County is misreading what is said. Where the competence of both sides is at issue each side can be examined on that. But that is not the case here. The competence of the father is not in issue. The last sentence of the quote does not mean that if a defendant's competence is at issue that the plaintiff can be required to give opinion evidence about that field, whatever it is. That is a misreading of the case. The County also suggests that the father could be an expert witness at the trial. There is no evidence to support that submission and counsel for the plaintiff did not say that the father might give expert testimony. Of course that does not matter. We are talking about an examination for discovery of a litigant, not of an expert witness. The Rules do not allow for the examination for discovery of possible expert witnesses. The coincidence that the father has expertise in road projects does not allow him to be examined as a possible expert witness. Rule 200 does not have that scope. Rohr v. Hosack (1991), 119 A.R. 177 at 181-82 (Master). In Nicholson v. McCulloch (1971), 21 D.L.R. (3d) 126 (Alta. T.D.), Lieberman J. (as he then was) concluded that in a medical malpractice action a defendant surgeon could be compelled to answer questions at discovery which elicited his opinion about matters within his expertise and which related to issues in the lawsuit. He distinguished between that situation and one in which an ordinary witness was asked an opinion. At pp. 127-28, His Lordship said: Counsel for the defendant relies upon the judgments of the Appellate Division of this Court in MacGregor v. C.P.R., [1938] 3 D.L.R. 687 … and in Borys v. C.P.R. Co. and Imperial Oil Ltd., [1950] 1 W.W.R. 1093, as authority for the proposition that a person on examination for discovery cannot be compelled to answer questions directed at eliciting his opinion. It is significant that in both of the above cases the questions in issue were directed at an officer of a company who was produced for examination for discovery and in my respecful judgment those cases can be distinguised from the the case at bar in that totally different circumstances existed and particularly in that the defendant herein is a surgical specialist and is being sued for alleged professional negligence within the field of his specialty. In Shickele et al. v. Rousseau (1966), 55 W.W.R. 568, the defendant, a medical doctor, was sued because he had allegedly administered anti-tetanus treatment negligently and at the wrong time. On his examination for discovery he objected to certain questions whereby his opinion as an expert was sought. Davey, J.A., of the British Columbia Court of Appeal says at p. 570: With deference to the contrary judgments of judges of first instance, on principle it is difficult to see why a party to an action that raises directly his professional or techncial advice or conduct should not be required to give, on discovery, his expert opinion on matters directly connected with the issues raised, where that opinion would be admissible and relevant at the trial. Specifically, in this case, the appellant should be required to answer pertinent questions concerning his opinion upon the incidence of tetanus, proper anti-tetanus treatment, and the time it should be given, the recogonized method of such treatment, the dangers involved therein, the safeguards to be adopted, general medical practice and opinion thereon, and like matters. The examination of a party on discovery about his opinion on technical and professional matters presents some dangers because those opinions in many cases will require an opportunity for reflection and study, which the witness will not have if the matters are not directly in issue, and lie on the periphery of the case, and so may not be foreseen. Where the matters are directly in issue, the witness ought not to be surprised at being asked for his opinion on them, and should be prepared to answer them. . . . . . In my judgment, compelling the defendant to answer the questions in issue does not violate the general principle enunciated in the MacGregor case and the Borys case. I respectfully agree with the above-quoted decisions of the British Columbia Court of Appeal and I order the defendant to answer the questions set out in the notice of motion herein. Nicholson v. McCulloch (1971), 21 D.L.R. (3d) 126 (Alta. T.D.), was applied by Master Breitkreuz in Yellowbird v. Lytviak (1998), 218 A.R. 393 at pp. 399-400 (Master). 15. Questions to Spouses … The Alberta Evidence Act applies to such evidence, and that includes s. 9. Therefore, any question framed in such a way that it asks a husband to disclose any communication made to him by his wife during the marriage may be met by a proper refusal to answer. Tiedmann v. Basiuk (1977), 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 12 (T.D.), at 16, per McDonald J. And McMahon J. said: It now appears that the defendant might seek to examine Mrs. Chalmers on at least three areas: 1) What the plaintiff communicated to her about the accident; 2) What she communicated to the plaintiff about the accident; 3) What, if anything, she saw or heard at about the time of the accident. Only the first is clearly within s. 8 of the Alberta Evidence Act and privileged, even on Examination for Discovery. See Tiedman v. Basiuk et al. (1977), 5 A.R. 435 (T.D.). That statutory privilege is not and could not be overridden by the broad scope of rule 200. Whether the other two areas can be the subject of proper questions will depend upon the specific questions and I decline to rule in advance on those. Chalmers v. Associated Cabs Ltd. (1994), 152 A.R. 306 at 309 (Q.B.). However, the privilege created by s. 9 does not apply widows, widowers, or divorced persons. In Layden v. North American Life Assurance Co. (1970), 74 W.W.R. 266 (Alta. Master), Master Hyndman held that a plaintiff who sued her late husband's life insurer was obligated to answer questions about words her husband had said to her. The learned Master held that the law in Alberta is that as stated in Shenton v. Tyler, [1939] 1 All E.R. 827 (Ch. D.). At pp. 271-72, the learned Master said: In the result Shenton v. Tyler decided that the privilege given to spouses by sec. 3 of the Evidence Amendment Act, 1853[which he held was substantially similar to the Alberta legislation] is statutory and is the only privilege and that there was no such privilege at common law. Moreover the section is to be construed strictly and does not extend to include widows, widowers or divorced persons, and, where it applies, it only extends to communications to, but not by, the party who is called upon to make disclosure. The privilege may be waived by that party without the other's consent. The rule applies to interrogatories as well as to evidence at trial. In Case v. Canaccord Genuity Corp., 2019 ABQB 257, 2019 CarswellAlta 694, 91 Alta. L.R. (6th) 274 (Master), Master Schulz said: [38] The Alberta Evidence Act, RSA 2000, c A-18 provides: 4. (1) The parties to an action and the persons on whose behalf the action is brought, instituted, opposed or defended are, except as otherwise provided in this Act, competent and compellable to give evidence on behalf of themselves or of any of the parties. (2) The spouses and adult interdependent partners of the parties and persons mentioned in subsection (1) are, except as otherwise provided in this Act, competent and compellable to give evidence on behalf of any of the parties. […] 8. A spouse or an adult interdependent partner is not compellable to disclose any communication made to him or her by the other spouse or adult interdependent partner during the marriage or adult interdependent relationship. [39] As described by the Alberta Court of Appeal in R v Legge, 2014 ABCA 213 (CanLII) at para 39 (“Legge”), “[t]he Alberta Evidence Act abolishes the spousal immunity rule in civil proceedings in Alberta and creates a “spousal privilege” that protects communications between spouses during the course of their marriage from being forcibly disclosed”. Defendant's Position [40] The Defendant cites Whyte v Armstrong (1990), 1990 CanLII 1079 (BC SC), 46 BCLR (2d) 36 (BCSC) (“Whyte”), a case where the British Columbia Superior Court considered its equivalent provision relating to spousal privilege. The plaintiffs, a husband and a wife, alleged that they and the defendants had entered into two oral agreements to become partners in two ventures to acquire and operate automobile dealerships. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants breached the partnership agreements, resulting in damage to them both. It was understood that the wife did not take part in any negotiations, oral agreements, or business dealings. Her limited role included contributing to the purchase price and acquiring shares. On examination for discovery, the wife stated she had no knowledge of the agreement besides what her husband had told her. She claimed marital privilege and declined to answer any questions relating to conversations she had with her husband concerning the agreements alleged in the statement of claim. Ultimately, the Court determined that “a litigant cannot claim a privilege where … she has put into issue the very matters which are then sought to be clothed with the privilege”: Whyte at paragraph 13. The Court continued at paragraphs 14 and 15: 14 In determining whether the status of a spouse as litigant is sufficient to waive the spousal privilege which would otherwise prevail, it is necessary to weigh the competing policy considerations. On the one hand, spousal privilege is grounded upon policy considerations designed to foster the harmony and sanctity of the marriage relationship. On the other hand, litigants are required to disclose all relevant, non-privileged communications on the policy basis that full disclosure is essential to justice. 15 In my view, justice requires that the spousal privilege give way to the latter policy considerations. A party who elects to be a plaintiff and raise certain issues cannot then elect to call upon a privilege to resist disclosure of relevant communications. The spousal privilege was never intended to have that result. [41] In essence, a Court should weigh the public interest in marital harmony requiring non-disclosure against the interest of justice requiring full disclosure of relevant information. … [48] The Alberta Court of Appeal in Legge is clear that, bearing in mind the provisions of the Alberta Evidence Act, communications between spouses cannot be forcibly disclosed. However, as explained in Whyte, the justice of a case sometimes requires spousal privilege to give way to the need for disclosure of relevant communications. [49] Both Stanley and Maryann are plaintiffs in this action and have exposed themselves to the possibility of being questioned to matters directly relevant to their claim. A strict interpretation of the spousal privilege rule would suggest that each spouse can be questioned regarding facts known to them, however, not questioned on the discussions taking place between them with respect to those facts. The Plaintiffs recognize in their pleadings that Stanley was authorized to administer the Case Accounts for the family. In my view, the facts disclosed during discussions between Stanley and Maryann with respect to the managing of the Case Accounts, are crucial to both the Plaintiffs' action, and the Defendant's defence and third party claim. [50] This is an appropriate situation to apply the exception to spousal privilege described in Whyte. Regardless of whether the discussions between Stanley and Maryann were explicitly raised by the Plaintiffs, they are necessarily implicated by virtue of the claim. They have put into issue the very matters which are then sought to be clothed with the privilege. I conclude full disclosure of all relevant information in this case outweighs the policy rationale for spousal privilege. This conclusion is to be consistent with the Alberta Court of Appeal's commentary on the Court's power under r 5.1(2) in Alexander v Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada, 2016 ABCA 2 (CanLII), O'Ferrall, dissenting: Rule 5.1(2) authorizes the court to give directions or make any order required to achieve the purposes of Part 5 of the Rules which deal with disclosure of information. The purposes of Part 5 are that of obtaining evidence, encouraging disclosure of records, facilitating the evaluation of the parties' positions, resolving issues in dispute and discouraging conduct which unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings or unnecessarily increases costs. [51] Spousal privilege is waived in these circumstances. The facts discussed during the discussions between Stanley and Maryann should be disclosed. 16. Examination of Infants The decision of Strehlke v. Camenzind (1980), 27 A.R. 257 (Q.B.), is helpful. In that case, Mr. Justice Cawsey said at p. 271, quoting the Alberta Evidence Act[now R.S.A. 1980, c. A-21, s. 20]: Section 21 provides as follows: 21. (1) In a legal proceeding where a child of tender years is offered as a witness and the child does not, in the opinion of the judge, justice or other presiding officer, understand the nature of an oath, the evidence of the child may be received though not given upon oath if, in the opinion of the judge, justice or other presiding officer, as the case may be, the child is possessed of sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of the evidence and understands the duty of speaking the truth. (2) No case shall be decided upon such evidence unless the evidence is corroborated by other material evidence. (R.S.A. 1955, c. 102, s. 21). Rule 203 requires an examination for discovery to be taken before an examiner, who, in this instance, was the clerk of the law courts in Edmonton. Rule 203(4) provides that the clerk may rule on or make directions respecting the conduct of the examination. Strehlke v. Camenzind and R. 203(4) may be fairly taken as authority for the proposition that the clerk is an appropriate person to determine the matter of the child taking an oath. In that case, His Lordship went on to say at pp. 271 and 274: There was no evidence before me to suggest that at the time of the examination that the infants understood the nature of an oath and I had no way of knowing if, at the time of the examination, the infants were possessed of sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of their evidence and that at that time they understood the duty of speaking the truth … I am therefore of the opinion that the unsworn evidence of a child given at an examination for discovery pursuant to Rule 200 cannot be “read in” at the trial, because Rule 214 applies only to an examination under Rule 200, which does not deal with unsworn testimony and I adopt the reasoning of Ford, J.A., in Hebert v. City of Calgary where he states: that all questions of competency or capacity should have been determined before the examination is proceeded with. It might well be that the child would not be called as a witness at the trial and, even if he were, his intelligence and understanding may be quite different from that which he had at the time of the examination. 17. Use of Interpreters In Duro v. Toronto Dominion Bank (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 257 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Veit dealt with an application in which a party wished to question at examinations for discovery the opposite party's proficiency in the English language. Her Ladyship described the application at p. 258: The Toronto Dominion Bank applies to require Mr. Duro, who is not a native English speaker, to answer in English certain questions that were put to him on discovery. These questions relate to the conversations in English that Mr. Duro had with employees of the TD Bank. The Bank also wants to cross-examine Mr. Duro in English to test his English language skills. Mr. Duro is a native Italian speaker … With respect to cross-examining Mr. Duro about his skills in the English language and the use of interpreters, Her Ladyship said at p. 260: The Bank will not be allowed to test Mr. Duro's skills in English by requiring him to answer, in English, questions on that or any other subject. The Bank has not placed any evidence before the court on this motion that impugns the good faith of Mr. Duro in requesting an Italian interpreter. As the Ontario Court of Appeal indicated in Petrovic[R. v. Petrovic (1984), 13 C.C.C. (3d) 416], it is not for the court, much less for a party, to conduct a detailed inquiry into a party or witness' ability to speak or understand English unless some good reason is advanced for embarking on such an inquiry. That court also noted, properly in my opinion, that a court should be fair in its assessment of the need for interpreters: a person who may be able to get along in English sufficiently to meet the needs of employment may nevertheless require an interpreter for a trial where nuances or shades of meaning may be critical. Here, it is agreed that Mr. Duro is not a native English speaker. No evidence is provided by those who impugn his need for an interpreter. Neither of the defendants is entitled to conduct a detailed inquiry into Mr. Duro's ability to understand or speak English. The Bank is entitled, as it has done, to ask questions through an interpreter about Mr. Duro's experience as an English speaker. 18. Examination of Ministers of Crown (i) Generally As to the purpose of the rule, Mr. Justice Harradence stated: The purpose of R. 200 is to allow a party to gain information. It allows a party to examine an officer best informed and there may be cases where the person best informed is the minister. In those cases, the minister will be compelled to submit to examination. Where there are others beside the minister who are equally well informed, then policy dictates that those others should be examined. Leeds v. Alberta (Minister of the Environment) (1989), 68 Alta. L.R. (2d) 322 at 335 (C.A.). (ii) Onus In Hamilton v. Alberta (Minister of Public Works Supply & Services) (1991), 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 169 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Picard dealt with an application for an order compelling Minister of the Crown Isley to attend for discovery. At pp. 183-84, on the question of onus she said: The plaintiffs are required to satisfy this court that the Honourable Mr. E. Isley should be examined because this is a special circumstance and that he is the person best informed to answer questions relating to matters in issue in these proceedings. If there are persons equally well informed then, for policy reasons, the minister should not be examined … In my view, the initial burden is on the party making the application for an order compelling a minister or former minister of the Crown to attend at examinations for discovery to demonstrate that the minister is the person best informed. Should an applicant succeed, then to avoid an order being made, the Crown must satisfy this court that there are persons equally well informed. The fact that others may be knowledgeable is not, to my mind, conclusive of the matter. This seems clear from the passage taken from Elliott v. Holmwood & Holmwood Ltd. (1915), 9 W.W.R. 490 ([B.C. S.C.]) quoted with approval by Harradence J.A., at p. 331 of Leeds: It is not limited to the higher or governing officer only. The object of the rules is to discover the truth relating to the matter in question in the action, and the examination ought to be of such “officer” of a defendant company as is best informed as to such matters. [emphasis added by Picard J.] In Forsyth v. L.C., 2024 ABCA 14 at para. 17-23, the Court reaffirmed the law as set out above from Leeds v. Alberta (Minister of the Environment) (1989), 68 Alta. L.R. (2d) 322 at 335 (C.A.), and Hamilton v. Alberta (Minister of Public Works Supply & Services) (1991), 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 169 (Q.B.). 19. A Mayor of a Municipality Is Not an Officer or Employee In Olds (Town) v. McDonald, 2003 ABQB 682, 2003 CarswellAlta 1136, 333 A.R. 393, 17 Alta. L.R. (4th) 195, the defendant sought an order compelling the Mayor of the Town to submit to examination for discovery as an officer or employee (the Town had designated its Director of Corporate Services). Sulatycky A.C.J.Q.B. said at p. 397: “The provisions of the MGA[Municipal Government Act] lead me to conclude that a mayor of [a] municipality in Alberta is not an officer of the municipality so as to be compelled to submit to discovery.” His Lordship also concluded that a mayor is not an employee of his or her municipality. At p. 398, Sulatycky A.C.J.Q.B. said: The general scheme of the MGA is the creation of an elected body to guide and oversee the function of the municipality as administered by its staff of officers and employees. The separation of functions between councillors and employees is consistently reflected throughout the MGA. If any single section is determinative, it is s. 174(1)(j): 174. (1) A councillor is disqualified from council if ..... (j) the councillor becomes an employee of the municipality. Since the Mayor is a councillor, logic dictates that the Mayor is also not an employee. As the Mayor is neither an officer nor employee, I conclude that the Mayor is not compellable for discovery without a court order pursuant to Rule 200. At pp. 398-399, his Lordship also decided that: While the Mayor is not an officer or employee of the Town she may still be compelled to give evidence at discovery under R. 200.1(2). If, in the opinion of the court, a corporate party fails to select a proper representative, Rule 200.1(2) authorizes the Court to select a more appropriate representative. … Thus the Mayor is not exempt from being compelled to attend for discovery if (sic) by order if the Court is satisfied that the facts support such an order. 20. Questions Regarding Pleadings In my view, the question “upon what facts do you rely for paragraph X of your pleading” is always improper … An examining lawyer could properly say, “Paragraph 4(b) of your Statement of Claim alleges that the driver was impaired by alcohol at the time of the collision. Tell me all the facts about that impairment which you know or must properly inform yourself of”. There both the pleading and the question are factual, so the question is proper. If the questioner instead asks “On what facts do you rely for paragraph 4(b)”, the witness's lawyer may properly object. Then the questioner must decide whether he wants the opposing party's strategy or evidence or law (which he cannot get), or whether he simply wants facts (which he can). Here, we are dealing with employees and former employees. On its face, the Rule does not purport to limit examination of potential witnesses to the person or persons who are best informed. Indeed, such a notion contradicts the Rule because “best” is a superlative and suggests but one person in that category. Rule 200(1) places no limit on the number. Rule 200(2) expressly contemplates examination of more than one employee and the availability of more than one to examination for discovery. Rule 200(1)(c) only calls for “knowledge”, not any degree of knowledge. Additionally, the Rule refers to “persons who are or were employed by the other party”. The Alberta Rule, unlike rules in some other jurisdictions, does not refer to “servants” nor suggest that a true master-servant relation is required. Being “employed” by a company has been interpreted to be broader than being an employee of a company. Professionals, such as lawyers and independent consultants, can be “employed by” a company, for the purposes of discovery, without being legal employees of a company. The Cana decision describes the limiting factor as requiring a connection with the party as officer or employee. This case, a product liability action, is a good example of a proceeding where the matters raised in the pleadings involve a multitude of people in various capacities having dealt with the flawed product or components thereof. No one person is best informed in all aspects of the product. Determining who is best informed and on what issue presents unnecessary complications, particularly in a factually diverse and complex action such as this one. Judicial consideration of r. 200 has attempted to refine the “who” based on the circumstances of each case. Moreover, to require proof that the opposite party's employee is the one best informed before the person is examined puts the party seeking discovery in a Catch 22 situation. Several common threads can be gleaned from the authorities. They are as follows: 1. Whether a person fits through the “narrow gateway” must be determined on a case-by-case basis; 2. The burden rests on the party seeking to examine to establish a relationship akin to employment; 3. The person must have relevant knowledge acquired by virtue of that relationship; 4. The Rule should be given a wide and purposive interpretation as pretrial disclosure of relevant and material evidence is beneficial to the litigation process, facilitating settlement or narrowing the real issues in dispute; 5. The court should consider the nature of the functions performed by the person in question and whether they are broadly equivalent to those performed by traditional officers and employees. The list is not exhaustive. Omni Computer Services Ltd. There well may be cases where it is just and convenient for an examination for discovery to be held ex juris, and in such cases surely the court must have authority to name an out of province examiner. I would hold that in a proper case the court can name an examiner outside of the jurisdiction to enable an examination for discovery to be held ex juris. In considering whether to direct an examination outside its jurisdiction the court will ask whether it is “just and convenient” to do so. The relevant rules in Ontario and British Columbia expressly authorize examinations for discovery outside the jurisdiction if it is “just and convenient” to do so: G.C.C. Ltd. v. [68] Relevant circumstances in an application to exclude a party from discovery of another party can include the following, although some factors may be more important than others: a) the prejudice or unfairness to the excluded party, including limiting their right to be present at all aspects of a case to which they are a party: Lambert at para 9 citing Milgaard v Kujawa et al. (1995) 136 Sask R (QB); aff'd on appeal (1996) 1996 CanLII 4927 (SKCA), 137 Sask R 310 (CA); Kuefler at para 8; Foundation Group Mergers & Acquisitions Ltd v Norterra Inc, 1999 ABQB 442 (Master) at para 10; Speakman at para 1; Heasley v Labelle, 2013 ONSC 2601 at para 20; Sissons v Olson, 1951 CanLII 480 (BCCA), 1 WWR (NS) 507 at pp 509-511; b) whether co-parties have common interests or commonality of positions, although this is not enough on its own to justify exclusion: Lambert at paras 3, 9 and 28; Hykawy at para 6; St Peter v Deleavey, 2004 NBQB 364 at para 7; Besner v Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Ontario, 2011 ONSC 7335 (Master) at para 24, appeal dismissed 2012 ONSC 2258; Heasley at para 20; Lazar v TD General Insurance Company, 2017 ONSC 1242 at para 39; Keedi et al v The Wawanesa Mutual Insurance Company et al, 2020 ONSC 904 at para 26(f)(i); c) whether the co-parties are represented by the same lawyer, including because an exclusion order may compel counsel to cease to act for the excluded client: Lambert at paras 3, 10 and 28; Speakman at para 11; Besner at para 24; Lazar at para 39; Keedi at para 26(f)(ii); d) the degree to which credibility may be an important issue in the action: Lambert at paras 3, 9, 11, 18, 20, 22 and 36; Hykawy at para 6; Speakman at para 8; Sissons; The Atlas Corporation v Andy Ingriselli, et al, 2010 ONSC 3678 at paras 10-12; Besner at para 24; Lazar at para 43; Keedi at para 26(f)(iv); Dignazio et al. v. Weizman et al, 2005 MBQB 61 at paras 3 and 19, citing Chalmers v Chalmers, 1991 CanLII 11786 (MBCA), 75 Man R (2d) 48; St Peter at para 7(b); e) the risk of evidence being tailored or parroted: Lambert at para 3; Besner at para 24; Chafe v Baffin Run Limited, 2007 NLCA 53 at paras 10-20; Lazar at para 45; Keedi at para 26(f)(v); Twin Creek Dairy Ltd v Young's Equipment Inc, 2021 SKQB 57 at para 15; St Peter at para 7(d); f) the potential overlap or duplication of evidence of the party being questioned and the party sought to be excluded: Lambert at para 9; Besner at para 24; Lazarat para 39; Keedi at para 26(f)(iii); g) potential prejudice or unfairness to the party seeking exclusion, or the witness, if the order is not granted. For example, whether a party or witness is likely to be intimidated or unable to give evidence during the questioning: Besner at para 24; Kosowan at para 38; Krull; Heasley at para 20; and h) whether the proceedings are likely to be disturbed or disrupted: Heasley at para 20; Besner at para 24; Lambert at para 5, citing Sissons. Justice Marion then discussed the law governing when a party may be excluded from attending questioning on an affidavit. His Lordship said: [75] As with questioning for discovery, there is no specific rule in the Rules that provides for exclusion of a party from questioning on affidavits under rule 6.7…. … [98] In my view, a more nuanced approach is required. An appropriate approach to an application to exclude a party from questioning on affidavits is to apply the principles set out in Lambert and Hykawyby analogy, but modified for the unique nature of a questioning on affidavit. Therefore, the applicable principles are: a) parties have a right to be present at questioning on an affidavit under rule 6.7, subject to the court's discretion to exclude. The right to be present is particularly strong where the underlying relief involves an application for final substantive relief; b) the onus is on the applicant to establish an evidentiary foundation justifying exclusion; c) the focus is on the integrity of the legal process. The general test is whether exclusion is necessary for the fair and proper judicial conduct of the action; and d) one way the general test can be established is if the chambers judge is satisfied that there is a reasonable apprehension of misconduct or prejudice which, without an order, will defeat the object and purposes of questioning on affidavit. [99] Relevant factors in determining whether the applicant has discharged its burden include those previously mentioned above at paras [67]-[68] in respect of questioning for discovery, modified as necessary to the application/questioning on affidavit process. However, additional factors in this context of questioning on affidavits include: a) the nature of the underlying application. If the application involves final relief going to the substantive merits of the action, it is more akin to trial and is a strong factor against exclusion of a party. If the application is interlocutory or procedural, the case to resist exclusion may be weaker; b) the degree to which the apprehension or risk of evidence tailoring or parroting is mitigated by the fact that the affiants have already attested to facts; and c) whether exclusion will actually address the concerned mischief. The stage of the underlying action at the time of the application is important because it may affect whether the benefits of exclusion will have any practical effect. For example, if the evidence of the parties has already been fully explored in questioning for discovery or previous questioning on affidavits, without any restrictions on the availability or use of those transcripts, there may be little achieved through exclusion. Justice Marion's decision was unsuccessfully appealed. The Court of Appeal said: [9] On the merits, the appellant argues the chambers judge erred in law by failing to apply the correct principles and legal test regarding exclusion of witnesses from questioning on an affidavit. She argues the test from Lambert should have been applied. [10] The majority in Lambert determined that to displace a party's “inherent right” to attend questionings for discovery, the applicant must establish “on the evidence, that exclusion is necessary for the fair and proper judicial conduct of the action” [emphasis in original]. It provided, “That onus is discharged when the chambers judge is satisfied, on the evidence, that there is a reasonable apprehension that the object and purpose of an examination for discovery will be defeated” if the exclusion order is not granted [emphasis in original]. At issue in that case, as here, was the risk of evidence tailoring. The question was whether the applicant had established “a reasonable apprehension of testamentary misconduct”. The majority held there was insufficient evidence to support such an apprehension. As such, it set aside the subject exclusion order: Lambert at paras 3, 30-32. This Court in Hykawy at para 6 noted, “The key ingredient in the facts of [Lambert] was the absence of specific evidence that the various police defendants in that case would tailor their evidence.” [11] Before the chambers judge, the respondents argued a stricter onus should be applied where a party seeks exclusion from a questioning on an affidavit as compared to a questioning for discovery. The chambers judge accepted that the questioning for discovery cases could not be applied directly. We need not decide whether a more onerous standard should be applied, because we are satisfied – and the chambers judge found – that the appellant did not satisfy even the onus set out in Lambert. [12] The Lambert standard would require the appellant in this case to establish at least a “reasonable apprehension of testamentary misconduct”. The chambers judge found she had not done that, concluding at paragraph 122, “On balance, I find that Ms. Carbone has not discharged her onus, on the evidence before me, to establish a reasonable apprehension of evidence tailoring by the Defendants”. We agree with that conclusion. In the words of this Court in Hykawy, the “key ingredient” here is the complete “absence of specific evidence that the” respondents “would tailor their evidence”. 30. Presence of Non-litigants at Discovery In Foundation Group Mergers & Acquisitions Ltd. v. Norterra Inc. (1999), 246 A.R. 79 (Master), Master Funduk considered the question of non-litigants being present at the examination for discovery. At p. 81, the learned Master said: The basic rule regarding the exclusion of litigants from examinations is spelled out in Lambart v. Lomore (1997), 212 A.R. 182 (C.A.). Without more, litigants are entitled to be present at examinations. That applies to examination of other litigants as well as mere witnesses. That rule, which is a rule of exclusion, is not the issue before me… The issue before me is what I would call the “rule of inclusion”… Examinations for discovery are a private process. Without more, a non-litigant is not entitled to be present when a litigant is examined for discovery… Here the plaintiff is the applicant. However, the burden does not rest on the plaintiff to satisfy me that [the non-litigants] should be excluded. Rather, the burden rests on the defendant to satisfy me that [the non-litigants] should be allowed to be present when Anderson is examined for discovery. (That is why I call it a “rule of inclusion”)… The case law establishes that the court can, where it is appropriate, let a non-litigant be present when a litigant is being examined for discovery… Each case is fact driven. And at p. 84: … Convenience is not a sufficient reason. Labelling the [non-litigant] as a “resource person”… is almost an insult to a person's intelligence… It is not suggested, and more important there is no evidence to support it, that [the non-litigants] are “experts” or would be present at Anderson's examination for discovery to assist him in “very technical matters”… This is also not a case … where the presence of an expert was required to assist counsel. In Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v. Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2001 ABQB 99, 2001 CarswellAlta 140, 284 A.R. 386, a defendant applied for leave to have an Ontario lawyer who was not counsel of record attend during examinations for discovery to assist counsel in conducting the discoveries. Burrows, J. dismissed the application because the presence of the Ontario lawyer would only benefit the defendant. He concluded that “I cannot see that the ends of justice would be advanced in any respect by Mark IV being allowed to enjoy those benefits over Austec's objection.” He adopted the following principles as set out in Lynn v. Toronto General Trust Corporation and Cuddie, [1945] 3 W.W.R. 361 (Alta. S.C.). At p. 388, Burrows J. said: (1) That an examination for discovery is not open to the public. … (2) That the examiner has a discretion to admit or exclude persons desiring to be present according to the circumstances of the case and to what he considers calculated to secure the ends of justice. The term “examiner” refers to the person described in Rule 203(3). The decision in Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v. Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2001 ABQB 99, 2001 CarswellAlta 140, 284 A.R. 386, was considered but not followed in Ormiston v. Matrix Financial Corp., [2002] 9 W.W.R. 374 (Sask. Q.B.). In that case, Klebuc J., at pp. 380-381, set out the principles governing the presence of non-parties at discoveries: From the aforementioned and other authorities reviewed, I have extracted the following general principles applicable to the presence of nonparties at examinations for discovery: 1. Only the parties and their respective counsel, or in the case of the corporation, its agent, may attend an examination for discovery unless the parties have consented to the presence of a non-party, or the examining officer has granted the non-party leave to be present. In this jurisdiction, the local registrar or deputy registrar would normally be the examining officer, and failing them, a judge of this Court. 2. The examining officer and/or judge may exercise his or her discretion by granting leave for a non-party to assist at an examination in any of the following circumstances, which are not intended to constitute an exclusive list or to limit the discretion of aforementioned persons: (a) where the level of expert knowledge, technical, scientific or otherwise, relevant to the issues in an action is beyond the level of skill and knowledge normally expected of legal counsel and therefore legal counsel may be unable to conduct a proper examination without the assistance of an expert, specialist or technician. For example, the calculation of damages in a personal injury action is a matter that counsel should be able to address and therefore the presence of an accountant normally would not be permitted at an examination. The qualification of the expert assistant need not meet the thresholds applicable to experts testifying at trial. (b) a non-party who is not a professional expert concerning a particular complex issue before the court but who has the knowledge or abilities that will make the discovery process run smoothly and expeditiously, usually will be allowed to attend an examination for discovery in the capacity of an expert assistant. The ability to manage documents in an action involving a substantial number of documents, or familiarity with financial records, may be sufficient to warrant such person being given leave to assist at an examination; (c) where a party requires the assistance of a non-party in special circumstances; for example, an aged mother might be accompanied by her son or daughter. 3. The burden of establishing that a specific non-party should be allowed to attend at an examination for discovery rests with the party seeking the non-party's assistance. In most circumstances an affidavit setting out the applicant's needs, counsel's concerns and how the non-party can assist will be essential. 4. Where the applying party has met the requirements set forth in paragraphs 2 and 3, the burden of proving prejudice or other ground for excluding the non-party rests with the party opposing his or her inclusion from the examination for discovery process. What constitutes prejudice will vary from case to case. The issue was raised again before Burrows J. in Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v. Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2002 ABQB 349, 2002 CarswellAlta 440, 325 A.R. 1. In this application, the plaintiff wanted to examine for discovery a former employee (Mr. Gravelle) of the defendant, Mark IV Industries Ltd. (Mark IV). It was agreed that Gravelle would be examined in California, but he wanted his California lawyer present during the examination. Simply put, Gravelle was not prepared to have his interests protected by Mark IV's lawyer because there had been previous litigation between Gravelle and Mark IV. The plaintiff agreed with the California lawyer being present, but Mark IV did not. Burrows J. allowed the California lawyer to attend the discoveries. At p. 2, Burrows J. said: Mark IV objects on the basis that Mr. Robinson is not counsel for any party to the litigation and therefore has to right to be present. It refers to a previous decision in this action ([2001] A.J. No. 167, 284 A.R. 386) where I declined to permit a lawyer who was not a member of the firm which is counsel of record in this litigation to be present at the discovery to assist counsel for Mark IV over the objection of Austec. I held that a person who is neither a party, nor of counsel for a party, cannot be present at an examination for discovery without either the consent of the other party or the leave of the court. I observed that such leave will granted when it is in the interests of justice to grant it. I did not believe it to be in the interests of justice to grant leave in the situation then before me. However this situation is different. The party to be examined is a legal stranger to the litigation. There is good reason why he is not content to be represented by his former employer's counsel. There has been litigation between him and his former employer. In my view, even if there had been no such litigation, Mr. Gravelle should be permitted to have his own lawyer present if that is his wish. If a person who is not a party to the litigation wishes to have his own counsel present when he submits to cross-examination he should be afforded that right. In my view the interests of justice require that a person not be compelled to participate in any form of legal process without legal representation if he wishes it. I do not intend to suggest that a person required to participate in legal process is entitled to have the cost of legal representation paid by someone else. Indeed, I intend no comment on the question of who should bear the cost of the representation since that question has not been asked in this application. Mr. Gravelle will be permitted to have counsel of his choice present when he submits to examination for discovery by counsel for Austec as a former employee of Mark IV. 31. Exclusion of Previously Examined Employees A trial is open to the public while a discovery process is not. The non-litigant witness who is excluded at trial until he gives his evidence can remain in the courtroom after he has given his evidence because it is an open courtroom, i.e. open to the public. The non-litigant witness simply becomes a member of the public after he has given his evidence and so can remain in the courtroom on that basis. Because an examination for discovery process, or an examination of an employee under rule 200, is not open to the public the “open court” concept for trials is just not apt. There is no principled reason why an employee examined under rule 200 should have a right to be present to hear what is said by those that are examined after him. It does not take a rocket scientist to readily see that opposing counsel would set different dates for examinations of litigants and non-litigant witnesses to avoid people piling up in the examination room as “spectators”. An employee examined under rule 200 does not have a right to be present at the examination of those that follow him. Here too, arguments about evidence being tailored or not being tailored are just a red herring. Foundation Group Mergers & Acquisitions Ltd. v. Norterra Inc. (1999), 246 A.R. 79 (Master), at 85, per Master Funduk. 32. Court May Limit Hours of Discovery In Dunn v. Dunn (2000), 263 A.R. 197 (Q.B.), the plaintiff sought an order restricting the hours of the examinations for discovery. The filed evidence was to the effect that the plaintiff, due to medical reasons, was unable to participate in prolonged activities. Lee J. granted the order, and said at p. 200: The defendant notes that there are no case precedents for limiting the examinations for discovery of a witness. I too am unaware of a specific case to support the plaintiff's request. However, this does not mean that I am prevented from exercising my discretion to create an order limiting the time of discoveries. … …[T]here is no point in continuing with an examination for discovery where the witness is physically unable to assist the process. 33. Second Discovery There is, of course, power in the court to allow a second discovery of a party. Nonetheless, this discretion must be exercised judicially; second discoveries, merely for up-dates, should not be allowed as a matter of course. The defendants choose the timing of the plaintiff's discovery; they should normally be bound by the decision they make about that. One notes that there is a difference in the rules, and the application of the rules, between discovery of documents and discovery of people. As we know, discovery of documents requires constant updates: R. 195(2). However, we also note that it is not part of Alberta practice to require, during discovery of parties, the party being examined to give an undertaking to provide up-dates. It seems to me that the explanation for this distinction in treatment is explained by Stevenson & Côté in Civil Procedure Guide (1992), at p. 595; an undertaking to provide up-dates would be difficult to comply with and difficult to enforce. … here, no specific reason apart from the passage of time is given by the defendants for requiring an additional discovery of the plaintiff. In my view, this is not reason enough. Rudovics v. Misericordia Hospital (1994), 23 C.P.C. (3d) 85 (Q.B.), at 88-89, per Veit J. Wachowich A.C.J. has said: The Alberta Rules of Court are designed to balance the interests of opposing litigants and to ensure a fair system of justice to settle civil disputes. The Rules do not expressly limit a party to one examination for discovery. Rule 200 does imply a singular right, and that is indeed the practice. It is also the practice to except out undertakings and utilize words of adjournment to preserve a continuing right to discover. However, there is nothing in the Rules to require these practices. Therefore the court has jurisdiction to order a party be further examined or examined on more than one occasion. . . . . . In that [counsel] commenced examination for discovery and inadvertently appeared to conclude it in the face of the officer's unsatisfactory and incomplete answers, the comments of Master Quinn in Millinton v. Partec Lavolin Inc. (24 September 1985), Edmonton 8303-19789 (Q.B. Master) apply: The authorities indicate that where a solicitor has inadvertently failed to ask a question he intended to ask he would be entitled to ask such a question at a further examination. ..... When an examination has been concluded, a court may order a second examination of a party only in “exceptional circumstances”… … amended pleadings [have been] found to be special circumstances… Hiring a new solicitor is not a special circumstance… Alleging incompetence of the former counsel also is not a special circumstance… Inadvertently failing to ask an intended question may be a special circumstance … … Vague and unsatisfactory answers are a special circumstance… On a review of the scant 18-page transcript, it is obvious that virtually no information on the issues was obtained, and further, the defendant's officer did not properly inform himself for the purpose of discovery. His answers, in my view, were vague and unresponsive, constituting in the circumstances of this case, “special circumstances” which would make it in the interest of justice to order a fresh examination. ..... Because of the special circumstances in this case, being vague unresponsive answers, it is in the interests of justice to order a fresh examination. What should be the scope of this examination? In [Kennedy v. Turner Wine Co., [1942] 2 D.L.R. 779 (Ont. H.C.)], the new examination was to be limited to questions asked or topics already canvassed. Limiting the fresh examination in this case in the same way would provide justice for both parties, balancing the need for full disclosure with the need to be able to rely upon the expectation that parties' counsel are acting with their clients' authority and are doing so competently. However, Master Funduk found that the first examination was not in substance an examination for discovery. This finding I am not about to disturb. That is so, then I hold that the fresh examination should not be limited in any way, and should be conducted as though there had been no prior examination. Boulianne v. Two Hills No. 21 (County) (1996), 207 A.R. 150 at pp. 152-57 (Q.B.); [affirmed (1998) 219 A.R. 131 (C.A.)]. However, also note the comments in Reich v. Dewitz (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 410 (Master) referred to below in “Concluding versus Adjourning Examination”. 34. Concluding versus Adjourning Examination One must be careful when attempting to adjourn an examination for discovery. If the adjournment is not agreed upon by the parties, and if the court ultimately concludes that it was unjustified not to continue at that time, then one may find that the court considers the examination concluded and may decline to order a second examination. The more serious aspect of this matter is whether the plaintiff can have any further examination for discovery with reference to the matters which never were broached because of counsel's refusal to continue with the examination. Although Mr. Skinner spoke of adjourning the examination, the transcript says it was concluded. The Rules of Court do not contemplate more than one examination for discovery of individual litigants. The practice appears to be that an adjournment will be made to allow undertakings to be complied with and to allow any applications to the court concerning unanswered questions or refused undertakings. When those matters are dealt with the examination would resume and be completed. There is very little Alberta law on this matter. In Sobkow v. Andruchow, [1930] 1 W.W.R. 593 (Alta. Master), Blair M.C. held that where an examination for discovery had been concluded (and not merely adjourned) the examination was at an end and he declined to order the defendant to answer certain questions he had refused to answer. An appeal was made to Mr. Justice Tweedie who dismissed the appeal but stated he would give the plaintiff an order for further examination because the objection to answering the question had not been valid. In the present case the objection taken by counsel for the defendant was, in my view, valid and the basis for ordering a further examination does not exist. In any event counsel for the plaintiff would not want to be restricted to obtaining answers to the questions which were refused. He wants to have what would really be a second examination for discovery, because of what he believes was the unwarranted intervention by counsel for the defendant. Cominco Ltd. v. Westinghouse Canada Ltd. (1979), 14 B.C.L.R. 346, (S.C.), and Canalta Concrete Contractors v. Camrose (1985), 38 Alta. L.R. (2d) 153 (Master), are cases which discuss undue interruptions in cross examinations. These are very helpful cases on the proper conduct of counsel, but neither of them are cases in which a second examination was ordered where a counsel had of his own accord decided to terminate the examination… There may be some cases where conduct of opposing counsel is so obstructive and contumacious that examining counsel would be justified in refusing to continue and could obtain an order for a further or second examination. Reich v. Dewitz (1995), 30 Alta. L.R. (3d) 410 (Master), at 412-14, per Master Quinn. In Tecon Investments Ltd. v. Ottawa Algonquin Travel Corp., 2000 ABQB 506, 2000 CarswellAlta 741, 269 A.R. 333, the plaintiffs commenced the examination for discovery of one of the defendants (Greenwood), but adjourned it prior to its conclusion. The plaintiffs wanted to commence the examination of another defendant (Rourke) prior to completing the first defendant. In rejecting that approach, Veit, J. said, at p. 337: By leaving open the discovery of the defendant Greenwood, the plaintiffs are, effectively, giving themselves a second, or even an ongoing, discovery of that party. This is not allowed in our Rules, and for good reason. If a litigant were to take the same position as that taken by the defendants here, discoveries would never terminate because a litigant would never want to close off examination of one party until all other parties had been examined. This creates a vicious circle, vicious because it is never ending. The defendants are entitled to insist that the plaintiffs conclude their discovery of the defendant Greenwood before moving on to the discovery of the defendant Rourke. Also see the annotation under “Second Discovery”, supra. 35. Source of Information Irrelevant The defendant says that rule 200(1) must be read in two parts. Firstly, the words “acquired by virtue of that employment” describe the essential qualities of the person who is within the ambit of the rule and therefore can be examined for discovery. Secondly, the phrase “touching the matters in question” describe the scope of the Examination for Discovery of a person thus qualified to be examined. The plain reading of the language of the rule supports that interpretation. In British Columbia it has been held in Wallace Neon Ltd. v. Tilden Corp. et al. (1964), 47 W.W.R. (N.S.) 61 (B.C. C.A.), at p. 63: In my opinion, a witness being examined as an officer of a company must answer all such questions on matters of which he has personal knowledge, including his own conduct, regardless of the capacity in which he gained that knowledge, so long as it was gained during the time he held office or was employed by the company. I agree with the judgment of Middleton, J., to that effect in Kennedy v. Suydam (1915), 8 O.W.N. 65, although I desire to reserve for futher consideration the application of his reasoning to knowledge gained, or acts done, by the witness before he was appointed or employed, a question that does not arise here. There is no reason why the same logic ought not to apply employees… It would be retrogressive to now limit Examination for Discovery to only knowledge gained by the witness in one capacity and not another. Once a person is a proper subject of an Examination for Discovery, all that person's knowledge touching the matters in issue is within the scope of the Examination for Discovery. Where the person being examined is an employee, and has knowledge gained by virtue of that employment and also knowledge acquired outside that employment, the latter may or may not bind the employer or be attributed to the employer. That is for the trial judge to decide, but the source of the person's knowledge does not alone serve to limit the scope of the discovery. Chalmers v. Associated Cabs Ltd. (1994), 152 A.R. 306 (Q.B.), at 307-308, per McMahon J. In Gienow Building Products Ltd. v. Tremco Inc., 2000 ABCA 105, 2000 CarswellAlta 302, 255 A.R. 273, 78 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40, the issue before the Court was whether a former employee of a party can be examined for discovery about information which is relevant but was acquired after the employment with the party ended. Fruman J.A. said, at p. 52: “… relevant information acquired by a former employee while employed by a company other than Tremco [the party] was a proper subject of examination for discovery.” At p. 55, she reiterated: A former employee of a party who is a proper subject of discovery under R. 200(1) may be examined on all knowledge touching the matters in issue even though the information was acquired after employment ended. 36. Conduct of Counsel at Examination See related annotation under R. 6.20, “Conduct of Counsel at Cross-examination”, on Canalta Concrete Contractors v. Camrose (1985), 38 Alta. L.R. (2d) 153 (Master); although this deals with cross-examination on affidavits, it is relevant to examinations for discovery. 37. When should costs be paid under R. 5.17(2)? In Graham Group Ltd. v. Labas Estate, 2018 ABQB 848, 2018 CarswellAlta 2283 (Master), the Plaintiff “agreed to produce several employees for questioning” by the Defendant. The issue was when the Defendant would pay the costs associated with that questioning. Master Schlosser decided that the costs need not be paid “up front”. The learned Master said: [11] Both the rule and the decided cases affirm that the Defendant in this case will have to pay the costs for questioning these additional employees in any event of the cause. But in the absence of circumstances that might suggest that security would be appropriate, I am reluctant to order that the costs be payable up-front. At the very least, this might impair a set off at the end of the day.
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 7)

sentences.text: 1.2(1) The purpose of these rules is to provide a means by which claims can be fairly and justly resolved in or by a court process in a timely and a cost-effective way. … In particular, these rules are intended to be used to identify the real issues in dispute … to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense … and so on.
9 I find that the Master has erred in law for the reasons set out in the appellant's brief.

It is clear to me, as argued by the appellant, that the Master's order artificially limits questioning by Cenovus, creates unnecessary delay, undermines the efficiency and cost-effectiveness, and prejudices Cenovus' ability to obtain information.

In short, the Master erred in not allowing the questioning to occur concurrently, based on the availability of witnesses, which is the norm in litigation, and to my knowledge has never been other than what has been indicated in the appellant's brief.
It is for all of these reasons that the appeal is granted, and there are costs in favour of the appellant on the normal schedule.
Questions Going to Credibility In Yeung v.
303 (Master), the plaintiff commenced an action in replevin, alleging that the defendant had stolen certain items from the plaintiff.

In examinations for discovery, the defendant was examined as to her criminal record and the plaintiff sought an order of the court compelling the defendant to produce medical records which allegedly would show that the defendant suffered from a mental disorder.
In dismissing the application, Master Funduk, at p.
306 said: Clearly this is an abuse of an examination for discovery.
This is information sought to show that the defendant is not credible.
But matters going solely to credibility cannot be the subject of examinations for discovery.
What is the connection between those convictions and this replevin action.
There is none.
The medical testimony in the criminal proceedings is also not relevant.
It is sought to show that the defendant is a thief.
It is sought to show that she is not credible.
It is an attack on the defendant's credibility by an attack on her character.
That cannot be done on an examination for discovery where the person being examined does not raise her character as an issue in her pleading.
Questions about the Identity of a Witness In Hailmichael v.
Roodzant (1998), 72 Alta.
L.R.

(3d) 350 (Master), the plaintiff in a motor vehicle accident action, the trial of which was scheduled to last two weeks, learned that the defendant had located someone who claimed to have seen the accident occur.
The defendant would not disclose the name of the witness.
The plaintiff brought an application to compel disclosure.
In granting the order sought, Master Waller acknowledged that “the general rule is that the names of witnesses need not be disclosed” (p.
However, the learned Master noted an exception: the name will have to be disclosed “if the name of the person is a relevant fact in the case”.
That exception is itself qualified because disclosure will not be ordered “where the disclosure of the name of a witness might adversely effect (sic) that party” (p.
Master Waller then reviewed the law in Alberta, and noted that “there can be no doubt that the prevalent judicial view requires full disclosure through the discovery process” (p.
In refusing to follow previous decisions, and ordering disclosure of the witness's name, the learned Master said, at pp.
354-55: This requirement of full disclosure has manifested a number of rule changes including rules dealing with the disclosure of evidence of experts.
Indeed the Rules of Court Committee of the Law Society of Alberta have recommended changes to Practice Note No.
3 to allow a pre-trial conference [justice] to direct the disclosure of names of all witnesses proposed to be called.
The law is never static, it changes with the times and evolves to deal with current realities.
The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in Soke Farm Equipment Ltd. v.
