The chambers judge accepted that the questioning for discovery cases could not be applied directly.
We need not decide whether a more onerous standard should be applied, because we are satisfied – and the chambers judge found – that the appellant did not satisfy even the onus set out in Lambert.
[12] The Lambert standard would require the appellant in this case to establish at least a “reasonable apprehension of testamentary misconduct”.
The chambers judge found she had not done that, concluding at paragraph 122, “On balance, I find that Ms.
Carbone has not discharged her onus, on the evidence before me, to establish a reasonable apprehension of evidence tailoring by the Defendants”.
We agree with that conclusion.
In the words of this Court in Hykawy, the “key ingredient” here is the complete “absence of specific evidence that the” respondents “would tailor their evidence”.
Presence of Non-litigants at Discovery In Foundation Group Mergers & Acquisitions Ltd. v.
Norterra Inc.
79 (Master), Master Funduk considered the question of non-litigants being present at the examination for discovery.
At p.
81, the learned Master said: The basic rule regarding the exclusion of litigants from examinations is spelled out in Lambart v.
Lomore (1997), 212 A.R.
Without more, litigants are entitled to be present at examinations.
That applies to examination of other litigants as well as mere witnesses.
That rule, which is a rule of exclusion, is not the issue before me… The issue before me is what I would call the “rule of inclusion”… Examinations for discovery are a private process.
Without more, a non-litigant is not entitled to be present when a litigant is examined for discovery… Here the plaintiff is the applicant.
However, the burden does not rest on the plaintiff to satisfy me that [the non-litigants] should be excluded.
Rather, the burden rests on the defendant to satisfy me that [the non-litigants] should be allowed to be present when Anderson is examined for discovery.

(That is why I call it a “rule of inclusion”)… The case law establishes that the court can, where it is appropriate, let a non-litigant be present when a litigant is being examined for discovery… Each case is fact driven.
And at p.
84: … Convenience is not a sufficient reason.

Labelling the [non-litigant] as a “resource person”… is almost an insult to a person's intelligence… It is not suggested, and more important there is no evidence to support it, that [the non-litigants] are “experts” or would be present at Anderson's examination for discovery to assist him in “very technical matters”… This is also not a case … where the presence of an expert was required to assist counsel.
In Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v.
Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2001 ABQB 99, 2001 CarswellAlta 140, 284 A.R.
386, a defendant applied for leave to have an Ontario lawyer who was not counsel of record attend during examinations for discovery to assist counsel in conducting the discoveries.
Burrows, J. dismissed the application because the presence of the Ontario lawyer would only benefit the defendant.

He concluded that “I cannot see that the ends of justice would be advanced in any respect by Mark IV being allowed to enjoy those benefits over Austec's objection.” He adopted the following principles as set out in Lynn v.
Toronto General Trust Corporation and Cuddie, [1945] 3 W.W.R.
361 (Alta.
At p.
388, Burrows J. said:
(1) That an examination for discovery is not open to the public. …
(2) That the examiner has a discretion to admit or exclude persons desiring to be present according to the circumstances of the case and to what he considers calculated to secure the ends of justice.
The term “examiner” refers to the person described in Rule 203(3).
The decision in Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v.
Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2001 ABQB 99, 2001 CarswellAlta 140, 284 A.R.
386, was considered but not followed in Ormiston v.
Matrix Financial Corp., [2002] 9 W.W.R.
374 (Sask.
In that case, Klebuc J., at pp.

380-381, set out the principles governing the presence of non-parties at discoveries: From the aforementioned and other authorities reviewed, I have extracted the following general principles applicable to the presence of nonparties at examinations for discovery: 1.

Only the parties and their respective counsel, or in the case of the corporation, its agent, may attend an examination for discovery unless the parties have consented to the presence of a non-party, or the examining officer has granted the non-party leave to be present.
In this jurisdiction, the local registrar or deputy registrar would normally be the examining officer, and failing them, a judge of this Court.

The examining officer and/or judge may exercise his or her discretion by granting leave for a non-party to assist at an examination in any of the following circumstances, which are not intended to constitute an exclusive list or to limit the discretion of aforementioned persons:

(a) where the level of expert knowledge, technical, scientific or otherwise, relevant to the issues in an action is beyond the level of skill and knowledge normally expected of legal counsel and therefore legal counsel may be unable to conduct a proper examination without the assistance of an expert, specialist or technician.

For example, the calculation of damages in a personal injury action is a matter that counsel should be able to address and therefore the presence of an accountant normally would not be permitted at an examination.
The qualification of the expert assistant need not meet the thresholds applicable to experts testifying at trial.

(b) a non-party who is not a professional expert concerning a particular complex issue before the court but who has the knowledge or abilities that will make the discovery process run smoothly and expeditiously, usually will be allowed to attend an examination for discovery in the capacity of an expert assistant.

The ability to manage documents in an action involving a substantial number of documents, or familiarity with financial records, may be sufficient to warrant such person being given leave to assist at an examination
(c) where a party requires the assistance of a non-party in special circumstances; for example, an aged mother might be accompanied by her son or daughter.
The burden of establishing that a specific non-party should be allowed to attend at an examination for discovery rests with the party seeking the non-party's assistance.
In most circumstances an affidavit setting out the applicant's needs, counsel's concerns and how the non-party can assist will be essential.

Where the applying party has met the requirements set forth in paragraphs 2 and 3, the burden of proving prejudice or other ground for excluding the non-party rests with the party opposing his or her inclusion from the examination for discovery process.
What constitutes prejudice will vary from case to case.
The issue was raised again before Burrows J. in Austec Electronic Systems Ltd. v.
Mark IV Industries Ltd., 2002 ABQB 349, 2002 CarswellAlta 440, 325 A.R.
In this application, the plaintiff wanted to examine for discovery a former employee (Mr.
Gravelle) of the defendant, Mark IV Industries Ltd.
(Mark IV).
It was agreed that Gravelle would be examined in California, but he wanted his California lawyer present during the examination.
Simply put, Gravelle was not prepared to have his interests protected by Mark IV's lawyer because there had been previous litigation between Gravelle and Mark IV.
The plaintiff agreed with the California lawyer being present, but Mark IV did not.
Burrows J. allowed the California lawyer to attend the discoveries.
At p.
2, Burrows J. said: Mark IV objects on the basis that Mr.
Robinson is not counsel for any party to the litigation and therefore has to right to be present.
It refers to a previous decision in this action ([2001] A.J.
No.

386) where I declined to permit a lawyer who was not a member of the firm which is counsel of record in this litigation to be present at the discovery to assist counsel for Mark IV over the objection of Austec.
I held that a person who is neither a party, nor of counsel for a party, cannot be present at an examination for discovery without either the consent of the other party or the leave of the court.
I observed that such leave will granted when it is in the interests of justice to grant it.
I did not believe it to be in the interests of justice to grant leave in the situation then before me.
However this situation is different.
The party to be examined is a legal stranger to the litigation.
There is good reason why he is not content to be represented by his former employer's counsel.
There has been litigation between him and his former employer.
In my view, even if there had been no such litigation, Mr.
Gravelle should be permitted to have his own lawyer present if that is his wish.
If a person who is not a party to the litigation wishes to have his own counsel present when he submits to cross-examination he should be afforded that right.
In my view the interests of justice require that a person not be compelled to participate in any form of legal process without legal representation if he wishes it.
I do not intend to suggest that a person required to participate in legal process is entitled to have the cost of legal representation paid by someone else.
Indeed, I intend no comment on the question of who should bear the cost of the representation since that question has not been asked in this application.
Mr.
Gravelle will be permitted to have counsel of his choice present when he submits to examination for discovery by counsel for Austec as a former employee of Mark IV.
Exclusion of Previously Examined Employees A trial is open to the public while a discovery process is not.
The non-litigant witness who is excluded at trial until he gives his evidence can remain in the courtroom after he has given his evidence because it is an open courtroom, i.e. open to the public.
The non-litigant witness simply becomes a member of the public after he has given his evidence and so can remain in the courtroom on that basis.
Because an examination for discovery process, or an examination of an employee under rule 200, is not open to the public the “open court” concept for trials is just not apt.
There is no principled reason why an employee examined under rule 200 should have a right to be present to hear what is said by those that are examined after him.

It does not take a rocket scientist to readily see that opposing counsel would set different dates for examinations of litigants and non-litigant witnesses to avoid people piling up in the examination room as “spectators”.
An employee examined under rule 200 does not have a right to be present at the examination of those that follow him.
Here too, arguments about evidence being tailored or not being tailored are just a red herring.
Foundation Group Mergers & Acquisitions Ltd. v.
Norterra Inc.
79 (Master), at 85, per Master Funduk.
Court May Limit Hours of Discovery In Dunn v.
197 (Q.B.), the plaintiff sought an order restricting the hours of the examinations for discovery.
The filed evidence was to the effect that the plaintiff, due to medical reasons, was unable to participate in prolonged activities.
Lee J. granted the order, and said at p.
200: The defendant notes that there are no case precedents for limiting the examinations for discovery of a witness.
I too am unaware of a specific case to support the plaintiff's request.

However, this does not mean that I am prevented from exercising my discretion to create an order limiting the time of discoveries. … …[T]here is no point in continuing with an examination for discovery where the witness is physically unable to assist the process.
Second Discovery There is, of course, power in the court to allow a second discovery of a party.
Nonetheless, this discretion must be exercised judicially; second discoveries, merely for up-dates, should not be allowed as a matter of course.
The defendants choose the timing of the plaintiff's discovery; they should normally be bound by the decision they make about that.
One notes that there is a difference in the rules, and the application of the rules, between discovery of documents and discovery of people.
As we know, discovery of documents requires constant updates: R.
However, we also note that it is not part of Alberta practice to require, during discovery of parties, the party being examined to give an undertaking to provide up-dates.
It seems to me that the explanation for this distinction in treatment is explained by Stevenson & Côté in Civil Procedure Guide (1992), at p.

595; an undertaking to provide up-dates would be difficult to comply with and difficult to enforce. … here, no specific reason apart from the passage of time is given by the defendants for requiring an additional discovery of the plaintiff.
In my view, this is not reason enough.
Rudovics v.
Misericordia Hospital (1994), 23 C.P.C.
(3d) 85 (Q.B.), at 88-89, per Veit J.
Wachowich A.C.J. has said: The Alberta Rules of Court are designed to balance the interests of opposing litigants and to ensure a fair system of justice to settle civil disputes.
The Rules do not expressly limit a party to one examination for discovery.
Rule 200 does imply a singular right, and that is indeed the practice.
It is also the practice to except out undertakings and utilize words of adjournment to preserve a continuing right to discover.
However, there is nothing in the Rules to require these practices.
Therefore the court has jurisdiction to order a party be further examined or examined on more than one occasion. . . . . .

In that [counsel] commenced examination for discovery and inadvertently appeared to conclude it in the face of the officer's unsatisfactory and incomplete answers, the comments of Master Quinn in Millinton v.
Partec Lavolin Inc.
(24 September 1985), Edmonton 8303-19789 (Q.B.

Master) apply: The authorities indicate that where a solicitor has inadvertently failed to ask a question he intended to ask he would be entitled to ask such a question at a further examination. .....

When an examination has been concluded, a court may order a second examination of a party only in “exceptional circumstances”… … amended pleadings [have been] found to be special circumstances… Hiring a new solicitor is not a special circumstance… Alleging incompetence of the former counsel also is not a special circumstance… Inadvertently failing to ask an intended question may be a special circumstance … … Vague and unsatisfactory answers are a special circumstance… On a review of the scant 18-page transcript, it is obvious that virtually no information on the issues was obtained, and further, the defendant's officer did not properly inform himself for the purpose of discovery.

His answers, in my view, were vague and unresponsive, constituting in the circumstances of this case, “special circumstances” which would make it in the interest of justice to order a fresh examination. .....
Because of the special circumstances in this case, being vague unresponsive answers, it is in the interests of justice to order a fresh examination.
What should be the scope of this examination?
In [Kennedy v.
Turner Wine Co., [1942] 2 D.L.R.
H.C.)], the new examination was to be limited to questions asked or topics already canvassed.

Limiting the fresh examination in this case in the same way would provide justice for both parties, balancing the need for full disclosure with the need to be able to rely upon the expectation that parties' counsel are acting with their clients' authority and are doing so competently.
However, Master Funduk found that the first examination was not in substance an examination for discovery.
This finding I am not about to disturb.
That is so, then I hold that the fresh examination should not be limited in any way, and should be conducted as though there had been no prior examination.
Boulianne v.
Two Hills No.
150 at pp.
However, also note the comments in Reich v.
Dewitz (1995), 30 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 410 (Master) referred to below in “Concluding versus Adjourning Examination”.
Concluding versus Adjourning Examination One must be careful when attempting to adjourn an examination for discovery.

If the adjournment is not agreed upon by the parties, and if the court ultimately concludes that it was unjustified not to continue at that time, then one may find that the court considers the examination concluded and may decline to order a second examination.

The more serious aspect of this matter is whether the plaintiff can have any further examination for discovery with reference to the matters which never were broached because of counsel's refusal to continue with the examination.
Although Mr.
Skinner spoke of adjourning the examination, the transcript says it was concluded.
The Rules of Court do not contemplate more than one examination for discovery of individual litigants.

The practice appears to be that an adjournment will be made to allow undertakings to be complied with and to allow any applications to the court concerning unanswered questions or refused undertakings.
When those matters are dealt with the examination would resume and be completed.
There is very little Alberta law on this matter.
In Sobkow v.
Andruchow, [1930] 1 W.W.R.
593 (Alta.

Master), Blair M.C. held that where an examination for discovery had been concluded (and not merely adjourned) the examination was at an end and he declined to order the defendant to answer certain questions he had refused to answer.
An appeal was made to Mr.
Justice Tweedie who dismissed the appeal but stated he would give the plaintiff an order for further examination because the objection to answering the question had not been valid.
In the present case the objection taken by counsel for the defendant was, in my view, valid and the basis for ordering a further examination does not exist.
In any event counsel for the plaintiff would not want to be restricted to obtaining answers to the questions which were refused.
He wants to have what would really be a second examination for discovery, because of what he believes was the unwarranted intervention by counsel for the defendant.
Cominco Ltd. v.
Westinghouse Canada Ltd.
346, (S.C.), and Canalta Concrete Contractors v.
Camrose (1985), 38 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 153 (Master), are cases which discuss undue interruptions in cross examinations.

These are very helpful cases on the proper conduct of counsel, but neither of them are cases in which a second examination was ordered where a counsel had of his own accord decided to terminate the examination… There may be some cases where conduct of opposing counsel is so obstructive and contumacious that examining counsel would be justified in refusing to continue and could obtain an order for a further or second examination.
Reich v.
Dewitz (1995), 30 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 410 (Master), at 412-14, per Master Quinn.
In Tecon Investments Ltd. v.
Ottawa Algonquin Travel Corp., 2000 ABQB 506, 2000 CarswellAlta 741, 269 A.R.
333, the plaintiffs commenced the examination for discovery of one of the defendants (Greenwood), but adjourned it prior to its conclusion.
The plaintiffs wanted to commence the examination of another defendant (Rourke) prior to completing the first defendant.
In rejecting that approach, Veit, J. said, at p.
337: By leaving open the discovery of the defendant Greenwood, the plaintiffs are, effectively, giving themselves a second, or even an ongoing, discovery of that party.
This is not allowed in our Rules, and for good reason.

If a litigant were to take the same position as that taken by the defendants here, discoveries would never terminate because a litigant would never want to close off examination of one party until all other parties had been examined.
This creates a vicious circle, vicious because it is never ending.
The defendants are entitled to insist that the plaintiffs conclude their discovery of the defendant Greenwood before moving on to the discovery of the defendant Rourke.
Also see the annotation under “Second Discovery”, supra.
Source of Information Irrelevant The defendant says that rule 200(1) must be read in two parts.
Firstly, the words “acquired by virtue of that employment” describe the essential qualities of the person who is within the ambit of the rule and therefore can be examined for discovery.
Secondly, the phrase “touching the matters in question” describe the scope of the Examination for Discovery of a person thus qualified to be examined.
The plain reading of the language of the rule supports that interpretation.
In British Columbia it has been held in Wallace Neon Ltd. v.
Tilden Corp. et al.
C.A.), at p.

63: In my opinion, a witness being examined as an officer of a company must answer all such questions on matters of which he has personal knowledge, including his own conduct, regardless of the capacity in which he gained that knowledge, so long as it was gained during the time he held office or was employed by the company.
I agree with the judgment of Middleton, J., to that effect in Kennedy v.
Suydam (1915), 8 O.W.N.

65, although I desire to reserve for futher consideration the application of his reasoning to knowledge gained, or acts done, by the witness before he was appointed or employed, a question that does not arise here.

There is no reason why the same logic ought not to apply employees… It would be retrogressive to now limit Examination for Discovery to only knowledge gained by the witness in one capacity and not another.
Once a person is a proper subject of an Examination for Discovery, all that person's knowledge touching the matters in issue is within the scope of the Examination for Discovery.

Where the person being examined is an employee, and has knowledge gained by virtue of that employment and also knowledge acquired outside that employment, the latter may or may not bind the employer or be attributed to the employer.
That is for the trial judge to decide, but the source of the person's knowledge does not alone serve to limit the scope of the discovery.
Chalmers v.
Associated Cabs Ltd.
306 (Q.B.), at 307-308, per McMahon J.
In Gienow Building Products Ltd. v.
Tremco Inc., 2000 ABCA 105, 2000 CarswellAlta 302, 255 A.R.
L.R.

(3d) 40, the issue before the Court was whether a former employee of a party can be examined for discovery about information which is relevant but was acquired after the employment with the party ended.
Fruman J.A. said, at p.
52: “… relevant information acquired by a former employee while employed by a company other than Tremco [the party] was a proper subject of examination for discovery.” At p.
55, she reiterated: A former employee of a party who is a proper subject of discovery under R.
200(1) may be examined on all knowledge touching the matters in issue even though the information was acquired after employment ended.
Conduct of Counsel at Examination See related annotation under R.
6.20, “Conduct of Counsel at Cross-examination”, on Canalta Concrete Contractors v.
Camrose (1985), 38 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 153 (Master); although this deals with cross-examination on affidavits, it is relevant to examinations for discovery.
When should costs be paid under R.
In Graham Group Ltd. v.
Labas Estate, 2018 ABQB 848, 2018 CarswellAlta 2283 (Master), the Plaintiff “agreed to produce several employees for questioning” by the Defendant.
The issue was when the Defendant would pay the costs associated with that questioning.
Master Schlosser decided that the costs need not be paid “up front”.

The learned Master said: [11] Both the rule and the decided cases affirm that the Defendant in this case will have to pay the costs for questioning these additional employees in any event of the cause.
But in the absence of circumstances that might suggest that security would be appropriate, I am reluctant to order that the costs be payable up-front.
At the very least, this might impair a set off at the end of the day.
